title: CUET Political Science Test 10
subject: Political Science (Code: 323)
syllabus_source: CUET SYLLABUS/Political Science - 323.pdf (NTA syllabus for CUET (UG) 2026, latest published)
past_paper_reference: Pattern benchmark only: NTA CUET (UG) Political Science papers 2024 and 2026, analysed for format only (no questions copied)
textbooks: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence
instructions: Each correct answer earns 5 marks; each incorrect answer deducts 1 mark; unattempted questions earn 0.
One set of 5 questions is based on a passage; the set stays together.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: ASEAN members with which India signed free trade agreements
questions.question: With which two ASEAN members did India sign free trade agreements?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Singapore and Thailand
Why: NCERT notes that India signed free trade agreements with Singapore and Thailand.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are not the countries NCERT names.
Key point: India's Look East policy deepened economic ties with ASEAN.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: Not a principle of Bangladesh's first Constitution
questions.question: Bangladesh's first Constitution declared faith in several principles. Which of the following was NOT one of them?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Monarchy
Why: The Constitution declared faith in secularism, democracy and socialism; Bangladesh was never a monarchy.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) were all in the first Constitution.
Key point: Bangladesh soon moved away from these ideals under presidential and military rule.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Recent Issues and Challenges
questions.sub_topic: Politics of the 1990s — the false claim
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The New Economic Policy of 1991 was launched by the V.P. Singh government.
(B) The BSP began with Dalit support but later tried to win other social groups as well.
(C) Advani's rath yatra was stopped and he was arrested in Bihar in 1990.
(D) The word Hindutva literally means 'Hinduness'.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A) only
Why: Only (A) is false: the New Economic Policy was launched by the Narasimha Rao government in 1991.
Why not the others: (B) the BSP widened its base beyond Dalits. (C) Advani was arrested in Bihar. (D) Hindutva means 'Hinduness'. Options (B), (C) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: Mandal, Mandir and market reforms shaped the 1990s.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: Fear some neighbours have about SAFTA
questions.question: Why are some of India's neighbours suspicious of SAFTA?
options: A) They fear India will use it to capture their markets.
B) They think it forces them to adopt India's currency.
C) They believe it will stop all trade with China.
D) They fear it will make SAARC a military alliance.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) They fear India will use it to capture their markets.
Why: Some neighbours fear that India will use SAFTA to 'invade' their markets and gain influence.
Why not the others:
(B) SAFTA has no common currency.
(C) It does not stop trade with China.
(D) SAFTA is a trade agreement, not a military pact.
Key point: India's size makes neighbours wary even of economic cooperation.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: China, the EU and ASEAN — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) After 1949 China followed the Soviet model of state-owned heavy industry.
(B) China's market reforms were introduced under the leadership of Deng Xiaoping.
(C) The EU's members include several former communist countries of Eastern Europe.
(D) ASEAN's members gave up their sovereignty to a supranational government, as in the EU.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) Communist China first copied the Soviet model. (B) Deng Xiaoping led the reforms from 1978. (C) the EU took in many former communist states.
Why not the others: (D) is false: ASEAN works through informal cooperation (the 'ASEAN Way') and has not created supranational institutions. Options (C) and (D) include (D); option (A) leaves out (B).
Key point: ASEAN cooperates without giving up sovereignty.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: When India and China restored full diplomatic ties
questions.question: After the war of 1962, in which year were full diplomatic relations between India and China restored?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 1976
Why: Full diplomatic relations were restored only in 1976.
Why not the others:
(A) and (B) Relations were still frozen.
(D) 1988 is the year of Rajiv Gandhi's visit to China.
Key point: Relations improved slowly after 1962.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: The Soviet Union from 1922 to 2001, in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
(A) Soviet forces invade Czechoslovakia
(B) The USSR is formally established
(C) Soviet troops crush the uprising in Hungary
(D) The civil war in Tajikistan comes to an end
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (B), (C), (A), (D)
Why: (B) The USSR was established in 1922. (C) Soviet troops entered Hungary in 1956. (A) Czechoslovakia was invaded in 1968. (D) Tajikistan's civil war ended in 2001.
Why not the others: Option (A) puts Czechoslovakia before Hungary. Option (B) puts Hungary before 1922. Option (C) puts 2001 before 1968.
Key point: 1922 → 1956 → 1968 → 2001.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Environment and Natural Resources in Global Politics
questions.sub_topic: Countries with active forest movements
questions.question: NCERT notes that forest movements are active in the global South, in countries such as:
options: A) Canada, Norway, Sweden and Finland
B) Mexico, Chile, Brazil and Malaysia
C) Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Singapore
D) France, Germany, Italy and Belgium
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Mexico, Chile, Brazil and Malaysia
Why: NCERT names Mexico, Chile, Brazil, Malaysia, Indonesia, continental Africa and India as places with forest movements.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) are industrialised countries that NCERT does not name here.
Key point: Environmental movements are strongest where people depend directly on forests.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: What the Soviet economy had in abundance
questions.question: Which of the following was a strength of the Soviet economy?
options: A) A large market for privately owned shops
B) Free movement of capital to other countries
C) Vast energy resources and heavy industry
D) A strong lead over the US in consumer goods
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Vast energy resources and heavy industry
Why: NCERT says the Soviet economy had vast energy resources, including oil, iron and steel, and strong machinery production.
Why not the others:
(A) Private shops were not a feature of the planned economy.
(B) Capital did not move freely.
(D) The Soviet Union lagged behind the West in consumer goods.
Key point: The Soviet economy was strong in heavy industry but weak in consumer goods.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Regional Aspirations and Conflicts
questions.sub_topic: Regional movements and accords — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Sikkim's merger with India in 1975 followed a resolution of its Assembly and a referendum.
(B) The Naga National Council under Phizo declared independence from India in 1951.
(C) The Akali Dal formed coalition governments in Punjab in 1967 and 1977.
(D) The Mizo Accord was signed by Indira Gandhi and Laldenga.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) Sikkim's Assembly sought merger and a referendum endorsed it. (B) the NNC declared independence in 1951. (C) the Akalis led coalition governments in 1967 and 1977.
Why not the others: (D) is false: the Mizo Accord of 1986 was signed by Rajiv Gandhi and Laldenga. Options (C) and (D) include (D); option (A) leaves out (C).
Key point: Many regional conflicts ended in accords.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Crises of the Constitutional Order
questions.sub_topic: How some writers protested against the Emergency
questions.question: How did writers such as Shivarama Karanth and Phanishwarnath Renu protest against the Emergency?
options: A) By forming a new political party
B) By leaving India for good
C) By returning their state honours
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) By returning their state honours
Why: Karanth returned his Padma Bhushan and Renu returned his Padma Shri in protest.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are not what NCERT describes.
Key point: Cultural figures also resisted the Emergency.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: India's External Relations
questions.sub_topic: A parliamentary first after the 1962 war
questions.question: Which of the following happened in Parliament after the war with China in 1962?
options: A) The first no-confidence motion against a government was moved.
B) Parliament was dissolved and early elections were announced.
C) The Lok Sabha's term was extended by a constitutional amendment.
D) Nehru resigned and Shastri became Prime Minister at once.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The first no-confidence motion against a government was moved.
Why: The defeat led to sharp criticism of Nehru, and the first no-confidence motion was moved against his government in 1963.
Why not the others:
(B) No early election was held.
(C) The term was extended during the Emergency, not in 1963.
(D) Nehru remained Prime Minister until his death in 1964.
Key point: The 1962 defeat dented Nehru's standing.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Politics of Planned Development
questions.sub_topic: Landmarks of the planned economy
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) Bombay Plan
(B) Amul
(C) Bhilai
(D) Zamindari abolition

List-II
(I) Public-sector steel plant built with Soviet help
(II) Removed the intermediaries between cultivators and the state
(III) Drawn up by a group of big industrialists in 1944
(IV) Milk cooperative based in Anand, Gujarat
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why: The Bombay Plan was drawn up by industrialists in 1944 (III). Amul is the Anand milk cooperative (IV). Bhilai is a public-sector steel plant (I). Zamindari abolition removed intermediaries (II).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps the Bombay Plan and Amul. Option (B) swaps Amul and Bhilai. Option (D) swaps Bhilai and zamindari abolition.
Key point: Industry, cooperatives and land reform were all part of planned development.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Recent Issues and Challenges
questions.sub_topic: Government response to the Shah Bano judgment
questions.question: What did the government do after the Supreme Court's judgment in the Shah Bano case?
options: A) It appealed against the judgment to the President.
B) It brought in a uniform civil code for all citizens.
C) It passed a law in 1986 that overturned the ruling.
D) It referred the case to the National Human Rights Commission.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) It passed a law in 1986 that overturned the ruling.
Why: The government passed the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986, which nullified the judgment.
Why not the others:
(A) There is no appeal to the President against a judgment.
(B) No uniform civil code was introduced.
(D) The case was not referred to any commission.
Key point: Critics called the law appeasement, and the issue fed the Ayodhya debate.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Democratic Upsurge and Coalition Politics
questions.sub_topic: Why the Congress declined after 1989
questions.question: Why did the Congress lose its central place in Indian politics after 1989?
options: A) It was banned from contesting elections for a decade.
B) It merged itself into the Janata Dal in the year 1990.
C) It refused to take part in any coalition government.
D) Groups like the backward castes moved to other parties.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Groups like the backward castes moved to other parties.
Why: The Congress lost support among groups such as the backward castes, who turned to parties of their own, and so lost its broad social base.
Why not the others:
(A) The Congress was never banned.
(B) It did not merge with the Janata Dal.
(C) It later led the UPA coalition.
Key point: The Congress's 'rainbow' coalition broke up.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Era of One-Party Dominance
questions.sub_topic: Who led which opposition party in the 1950s
questions.question:
Match List-I (Leader) with List-II (Description).

List-I
(A) S.A. Dange
(B) Balraj Madhok
(C) Ram Manohar Lohia
(D) Acharya Kripalani

List-II
(I) Founded the Kisan Mazdoor Praja Party
(II) A leader of the Communist Party of India
(III) A Socialist leader and thinker
(IV) A leader of the Bharatiya Jana Sangh
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(III), (D)-(I)
Why: S.A. Dange was a CPI leader (II). Balraj Madhok led the Jana Sangh (IV). Lohia was a Socialist leader (III). Kripalani founded the KMPP (I).
Why not the others: Option (B) swaps Dange and Madhok. Option (C) swaps Madhok and Lohia. Option (D) swaps Lohia and Kripalani.
Key point: Several opposition leaders had once been in the Congress.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: India's External Relations
questions.sub_topic: India's wars and nuclear tests, 1947–1999, in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
(A) India and Pakistan fight their first war over Kashmir
(B) China carries out its first nuclear test
(C) The Kargil conflict takes place
(D) India carries out its first nuclear explosion at Pokhran
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B), (D), (C)
Why: (A) The first Kashmir war was fought in 1947–48. (B) China tested in 1964. (D) India's Pokhran explosion was in 1974. (C) Kargil was in 1999.
Why not the others: Option (A) puts China's test before the first Kashmir war. Option (C) puts Pokhran before China's test. Option (D) puts Kargil before Pokhran.
Key point: 1947–48 → 1964 → 1974 → 1999.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Globalisation and Its Critics
questions.sub_topic: A political effect of globalisation
questions.question: Which of the following is a political consequence of globalisation, according to NCERT?
options: A) MNCs gain a bigger role, so states decide less on their own.
B) States can no longer collect any taxes from their citizens.
C) Elections are now organised by international bodies.
D) All countries have adopted one common constitution.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) MNCs gain a bigger role, so states decide less on their own.
Why: The growing role of multinational companies reduces the ability of governments to take decisions on their own.
Why not the others:
(B) States still collect taxes.
(C) Elections remain national.
(D) No common constitution exists.
Key point: Globalisation can erode state capacity, though states remain important.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Politics of Planned Development
questions.sub_topic: What the government offered under the Green Revolution
questions.question: Under the Green Revolution strategy, the government:
options: A) took over all farmland and ran it as state farms
B) banned the use of chemical fertilisers in Punjab
C) stopped buying grain from the farmers of north India
D) gave cheap seeds, fertilisers and assured crop prices
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) gave cheap seeds, fertilisers and assured crop prices
Why: The government offered high-yielding seeds, fertilisers, pesticides and irrigation at subsidised prices and guaranteed to buy produce at a given price.
Why not the others:
(A) Land stayed with farmers.
(B) Fertilisers were promoted, not banned.
(C) The government guaranteed to buy grain.
Key point: State support drove the Green Revolution in irrigated regions.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: Why many republics resented the Soviet system
questions.question: Why did people in many Soviet republics feel resentment against the Soviet system?
options: A) Russia dominated, and other regions felt neglected and suppressed.
B) The republics were not allowed to use any machinery from Russia.
C) Every republic had to hold free elections with many parties.
D) The Soviet state forced them to join NATO and fight the West.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Russia dominated, and other regions felt neglected and suppressed.
Why: Russia dominated the Union, and people in other regions often felt neglected and suppressed, which fed nationalism.
Why not the others:
(B) The republics were part of one planned economy.
(C) The Soviet system was a one-party state.
(D) The USSR led the rival Warsaw Pact.
Key point: Nationalism in the republics hastened the collapse.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Nation-Building and Its Problems
questions.sub_topic: Not among the difficult princely states
questions.question: Most princely states joined India without trouble. Which of the following was NOT among the four whose integration proved difficult?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Mysore
Why: NCERT names Junagadh, Hyderabad, Kashmir and Manipur as the four difficult cases. Mysore joined without trouble.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) are among the four difficult cases.
Key point: Integration of 565 states succeeded with few exceptions.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Challenge to and Restoration of Congress System
questions.sub_topic: The Congress from 1967 to 1971 — the false claim
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The 1967 general election was the first held after Nehru's death.
(B) After the split, Indira Gandhi's Congress ran a minority government with the support of parties such as the CPI and the DMK.
(C) In 1969 the Syndicate supported V.V. Giri for President against N. Sanjiva Reddy.
(D) The Grand Alliance of 1971 included the Congress (O), the Jana Sangh, the Swatantra Party and the SSP.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C) only
Why: Only (C) is false: the Syndicate backed Sanjiva Reddy, the official candidate, while Indira Gandhi encouraged support for Giri.
Why not the others: (A) Nehru died in 1964, so 1967 was the first election without him. (B) the CPI and the DMK backed the Congress (R) minority government. (D) these parties formed the Grand Alliance. Options (A), (B) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: The 1969 presidential contest decided the split.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Era of One-Party Dominance
questions.sub_topic: Party that came second in votes in 1952
questions.question: In terms of votes, which party came a distant second to the Congress in the first general election?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Socialist Party
Why: The Socialist Party won just over 10 per cent of the votes, second to the Congress, though it won far fewer seats.
Why not the others:
(A) The Jana Sangh won only a small share.
(B) The CPI won more seats but fewer votes than the Socialists.
(D) The Swatantra Party was formed only in 1959.
Key point: Votes and seats did not match under the first-past-the-post system.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Security in the Contemporary World
questions.sub_topic: Why NCERT cites bird flu and mad cow disease
questions.question: Why does NCERT mention diseases such as bird flu and mad cow disease in the chapter on security?
options: A) To show that health threats can spread across borders.
B) To show that only poor countries face epidemics.
C) To show that disease can be dealt with by armies.
D) To show that such diseases have been wiped out.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) To show that health threats can spread across borders.
Why: These epidemics spread from country to country, showing that health threats are global and need cooperation.
Why not the others:
(B) Mad cow disease affected rich countries too.
(C) Armies cannot solve epidemics.
(D) These diseases have not been wiped out.
Key point: Epidemics are non-traditional security threats.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: Trouble spots after the Soviet break-up
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) Chechnya
(B) Tajikistan
(C) Nagorno-Karabakh
(D) Georgia

List-II
(I) Region of Russia where secessionist groups waged a violent struggle
(II) Province of Azerbaijan that wants to join Armenia
(III) Country where two provinces want independence
(IV) Central Asian country that suffered a civil war for ten years
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(I), (B)-(IV), (C)-(II), (D)-(III)
Why: Chechnya saw violent secessionist struggle in Russia (I). Tajikistan suffered a ten-year civil war (IV). Nagorno-Karabakh wants to secede from Azerbaijan and join Armenia (II). In Georgia two provinces want independence (III).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps Tajikistan and Nagorno-Karabakh. Option (C) swaps Chechnya and Tajikistan. Option (D) swaps Nagorno-Karabakh and Georgia.
Key point: The break-up left many unresolved conflicts.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: South Asian countries and their issues
questions.question:
Match List-I (Country) with List-II (Issue).

List-I
(A) Nepal
(B) Bangladesh
(C) Pakistan
(D) Maldives

List-II
(I) Has disputes with India over sharing river waters
(II) Has a dispute with India over Sir Creek in the Rann of Kutch
(III) A seven-party alliance led mass protests for democracy in 2006
(IV) Its politics is dominated by the Maldivian Democratic Party
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(IV)
Why: In Nepal a seven-party alliance led the 2006 protests (III). Bangladesh has river-water disputes with India (I). Pakistan disputes Sir Creek (II). The Maldivian Democratic Party dominates Maldives politics (IV).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps Nepal and Bangladesh. Option (B) swaps Bangladesh and Pakistan. Option (C) swaps Pakistan and the Maldives.
Key point: Each neighbour has its own issues with India.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: Odd one out among Southeast Asian states
questions.question: Three of these countries belong to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. Which one does NOT?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Sri Lanka
Why: Sri Lanka is a South Asian country and a member of SAARC, not ASEAN.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) are members of ASEAN.
Key point: ASEAN brings together the countries of Southeast Asia.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Era of One-Party Dominance
questions.sub_topic: Party that wanted India to have atomic weapons
questions.question: Which party called for India to develop atomic weapons, especially after China's test in 1964?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Bharatiya Jana Sangh
Why: The Jana Sangh argued that India should build atomic weapons, especially after China's nuclear test.
Why not the others:
(A) The CPI did not make this demand.
(C) The Socialists focused on economic equality.
(D) Swatantra focused on a free economy.
Key point: The Jana Sangh took a strongly nationalist position on defence.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Democratic Upsurge and Coalition Politics
questions.sub_topic: Turning points from 1980 to 2004, in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
(A) The Janata Dal is formed
(B) The Bharatiya Janata Party is founded
(C) Rajiv Gandhi is assassinated during an election campaign
(D) Manmohan Singh becomes Prime Minister
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (B), (A), (C), (D)
Why: (B) The BJP was founded in 1980. (A) The Janata Dal was formed in 1988. (C) Rajiv Gandhi was killed in 1991. (D) Manmohan Singh became PM in 2004.
Why not the others: Option (A) puts the Janata Dal before the BJP. Option (B) puts Rajiv Gandhi's death before the Janata Dal. Option (D) puts 2004 before 1991.
Key point: 1980 → 1988 → 1991 → 2004.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: India's External Relations
questions.sub_topic: What India's foreign policy strongly opposed
questions.question: India's foreign policy under Nehru strongly opposed:
options: A) the formation of the United Nations
B) trade with the countries of Asia
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) apartheid in South Africa
Why: India was a leading voice against racism and apartheid in South Africa.
Why not the others:
(A) India was a founding member of the UN.
(B) India sought closer ties with Asia.
(D) India supported Indonesia's freedom struggle.
Key point: Anti-colonialism and anti-racism were pillars of Nehru's policy.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Globalisation and Its Critics
questions.sub_topic: Sites and symbols of resistance to globalisation
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) Seattle, 1999
(B) Nairobi, 2007
(C) Neem
(D) Indian Social Forum

List-II
(I) Indian counterpart of the World Social Forum
(II) Protests at the WTO ministerial meeting
(III) Venue of the seventh World Social Forum meeting
(IV) Symbol of resistance to foreign patents on traditional knowledge
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(IV), (D)-(I)
Why: Seattle saw protests at the WTO meeting in 1999 (II). Nairobi hosted the seventh WSF meeting in 2007 (III). Neem became a symbol of resistance to foreign patents (IV). The Indian Social Forum is India's counterpart of the WSF (I).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps Seattle and Nairobi. Option (B) swaps Nairobi and neem. Option (C) swaps neem and the Indian Social Forum.
Key point: Resistance to globalisation is itself global.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Democratic Upsurge and Coalition Politics
questions.sub_topic: Why the National Front government lost its majority
questions.question: Why did the National Front government lose its majority in 1990?
options: A) The Left parties merged with the Congress.
B) The BJP withdrew its support after Advani's arrest.
C) The Supreme Court dismissed the Prime Minister.
D) The President dissolved the Lok Sabha on his own.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The BJP withdrew its support after Advani's arrest.
Why: When Advani's rath yatra was stopped and he was arrested, the BJP withdrew support and the government fell.
Why not the others:
(A) The Left did not merge with the Congress.
(C) Courts do not dismiss Prime Ministers.
(D) The government fell on a confidence vote.
Key point: Governments that depend on outside support are fragile.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Challenge to and Restoration of Congress System
questions.sub_topic: State that K. Kamaraj had led
questions.question: K. Kamaraj, who as Congress President played a key role in choosing Prime Ministers, had earlier been the Chief Minister of ________.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Madras
Why: Kamaraj had been Chief Minister of Madras (now Tamil Nadu).
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) were not led by Kamaraj.
Key point: Kamaraj was a powerful leader of the Syndicate.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Crises of the Constitutional Order
questions.sub_topic: Janata Party's own tally in 1977
questions.question: In the 1977 Lok Sabha election, how many seats did the Janata Party win on its own?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 295
Why: The Janata Party won 295 seats on its own, and 330 together with its allies.
Why not the others:
(A) 154 was roughly the Congress tally.
(B) 352 was the Congress (R) tally in 1971.
(C) 330 was the total for the Janata Party and its allies.
Key point: 1977 brought the first non-Congress government at the Centre.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Regional Aspirations and Conflicts
questions.sub_topic: Title of Sikkim's former ruler
questions.question: Before it merged with India, Sikkim was ruled by a hereditary monarch known as the ________.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Chogyal
Why: Sikkim's monarch was called the Chogyal.
Why not the others:
(B) The Nizam ruled Hyderabad.
(C) Maharana was a title of some Rajput rulers.
(D) Nawab was a title of some Muslim rulers.
Key point: Sikkim moved from monarchy to democracy and merger in 1975.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Environment and Natural Resources in Global Politics
questions.sub_topic: Environment and global politics — the false claim
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The Kyoto Protocol was based on the principles set out in the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change.
(B) The 'global North' refers mainly to the industrialised countries.
(C) Antarctica is owned and governed by the United States.
(D) Environmental issues began to gain international attention from the 1960s.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C) only
Why: Only (C) is false: Antarctica is a global common, governed under international treaties, not owned by any one country.
Why not the others: (A) Kyoto built on the UNFCCC. (B) the North means the industrialised countries. (D) environmental concerns grew from the 1960s. Options (A), (B) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: Global commons belong to no single state.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Globalisation and Its Critics
questions.sub_topic: A positive side of cultural globalisation
questions.question: According to NCERT, outside cultural influences can also:
options: A) wipe out every local custom within a generation
B) widen our choices and enrich our own culture
C) make a country's own language illegal
D) stop people from travelling abroad at all
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) widen our choices and enrich our own culture
Why: NCERT says external influences can enlarge our choices and sometimes modify our culture without overwhelming traditions.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) exaggerate or misstate the effects.
Key point: Cultural globalisation is not always negative.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Nation-Building and Its Problems
questions.sub_topic: Aim of the Vishalandhra movement
questions.question: What did the Vishalandhra movement demand?
options: A) The merger of Hyderabad with the State of Bombay
B) A separate State for Telugu speakers out of Madras
C) The transfer of Chandigarh to the State of Punjab
D) Autonomy for the tribal areas of the North-East
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) A separate State for Telugu speakers out of Madras
Why: The Vishalandhra movement demanded that the Telugu-speaking areas be separated from Madras province to form a new State.
Why not the others:
(A) No such merger was demanded.
(C) Chandigarh concerns Punjab and Haryana.
(D) The North-East is not linked to this movement.
Key point: The Telugu demand led to the first linguistic State.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Crises of the Constitutional Order
questions.sub_topic: Figures from the Emergency years
questions.question:
Match List-I (Person) with List-II (Description).

List-I
(A) A.N. Ray
(B) Raj Narain
(C) J.C. Shah
(D) Sanjay Gandhi

List-II
(I) Headed the commission of inquiry into the excesses of the Emergency
(II) Defeated Indira Gandhi at Rae Bareli in 1977
(III) Wielded great power without holding any official post
(IV) Appointed Chief Justice in 1973, superseding three senior judges
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(IV), (B)-(II), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
Why: A.N. Ray was made Chief Justice superseding three judges (IV). Raj Narain defeated Indira Gandhi at Rae Bareli (II). Justice J.C. Shah headed the inquiry commission (I). Sanjay Gandhi wielded power without any office (III).
Why not the others: Option (B) swaps Ray and Raj Narain. Option (C) swaps Raj Narain and Shah. Option (D) swaps Shah and Sanjay Gandhi.
Key point: The Emergency years raised questions about institutions and unaccountable power.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Challenge to and Restoration of Congress System
questions.sub_topic: What boosted Indira Gandhi's popularity after 1971
questions.question: Indira Gandhi's popularity rose further soon after the 1971 Lok Sabha election mainly because of:
options: A) the abolition of the Planning Commission
B) the success of the Grand Alliance
C) the end of the Emergency in that year
D) India's victory in the Bangladesh war
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) India's victory in the Bangladesh war
Why: India's decisive victory in the Bangladesh war in December 1971 added greatly to her popularity, and the Congress swept the State elections of 1972.
Why not the others:
(A) The Planning Commission continued until 2015.
(B) The Grand Alliance was her opponent and was defeated.
(C) The Emergency came later, in 1975.
Key point: Electoral victory and war victory together made Indira Gandhi dominant.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Regional Aspirations and Conflicts
questions.sub_topic: What fuelled militancy in Kashmir in the late 1980s
questions.question: Which development in Jammu and Kashmir is widely seen as having fuelled militancy from 1989?
options: A) The merger of Ladakh with Himachal Pradesh
B) The abolition of the State Assembly in 1975
C) The banning of the National Conference in 1980
D) Alleged rigging of the 1987 Assembly election
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Alleged rigging of the 1987 Assembly election
Why: The 1987 Assembly election was widely believed to have been rigged, which fed popular anger and militancy.
Why not the others:
(A) Ladakh was not merged with Himachal Pradesh.
(B) The Assembly was not abolished in 1975.
(C) The National Conference was not banned.
Key point: Denial of democracy fed alienation in Kashmir.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Nation-Building and Its Problems
questions.sub_topic: Integration and reorganisation — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The British declared that with the end of their rule, paramountcy would lapse and princely states could choose their future.
(B) Sardar Patel, as Deputy Prime Minister and Home Minister, led the integration of the princely states.
(C) Before 1960, the State of Bombay was bilingual, with Gujarati and Marathi speakers.
(D) Hyderabad was the smallest of the princely states and was surrounded by Pakistan.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) the British said paramountcy would lapse, leaving states free to choose. (B) Patel led integration as Deputy PM and Home Minister. (C) Bombay was a bilingual State until 1960.
Why not the others: (D) is false: Hyderabad was the largest princely state and was surrounded entirely by Indian territory. Options (B) and (C) include (D); option (A) leaves out (C).
Key point: Integration came first, and reorganisation of States followed.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Security in the Contemporary World
questions.sub_topic: Arms treaties and global crises, 1991–2003, in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
(A) The US and Russia sign START II
(B) The SARS epidemic breaks out
(C) Genocide takes place in Rwanda
(D) The US and the USSR sign START I
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (D), (A), (C), (B)
Why: (D) START I was signed in 1991. (A) START II was signed in 1993. (C) The Rwandan genocide took place in 1994. (B) SARS broke out in 2003.
Why not the others: Option (A) puts START II before START I. Option (C) puts Rwanda before START II. Option (D) puts SARS before Rwanda.
Key point: 1991 → 1993 → 1994 → 2003.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: Pakistan's leader after the 1971 defeat
questions.question: Who came to power in Pakistan after its defeat in the Bangladesh war of 1971?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Zulfikar Ali Bhutto
Why: After the defeat, Zulfikar Ali Bhutto led an elected government in Pakistan.
Why not the others:
(A) Ayub Khan had already given way to Yahya Khan.
(B) Zia overthrew Bhutto in 1977.
(D) Musharraf took power in 1999.
Key point: Bhutto's civilian rule ended in another military coup.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Security in the Contemporary World
questions.sub_topic: Narrow and broad views of human security
questions.question: How does the broad view of human security differ from the narrow view?
options: A) It deals only with threats from foreign armies.
B) It leaves out violence against individuals.
C) It covers the security of states but not of people.
D) It adds threats like hunger and disease to violence.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) It adds threats like hunger and disease to violence.
Why: The narrow view focuses on violent threats to individuals; the broad view adds threats such as hunger, disease and natural disasters.
Why not the others:
(A) Both views focus on individuals, not foreign armies.
(B) Violence is included in both.
(C) Human security is about people rather than states.
Key point: Human security puts people first.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: Why critics say the Council is out of date
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

The structure of the UN Security Council still reflects the distribution of power in the world as it stood in 1945. Since then the membership of the United Nations has grown from 51 to 193 states, many of them newly independent countries of Asia, Africa and Latin America, yet the Council has been enlarged only once. Critics say that the developing world is poorly represented in the body that takes the most important decisions on peace and security. Proposals for reform include adding new permanent members, adding more non-permanent members, or both, and there is a long debate about which criteria should decide who deserves a seat. The veto is an even harder question: some want it abolished or limited, while the permanent members are unwilling to give it up. India argues that, as the world's largest democracy, home to about one-fifth of humanity, with a growing economy and a long record in peacekeeping, it should be a permanent member. Any change, however, requires an amendment to the UN Charter, which must be approved by two-thirds of the members, including all five permanent members. This is why, despite years of debate, the Council looks much as it did decades ago.

Question: According to the passage, the structure of the Security Council reflects:
options: A) the balance of power that emerged at the end of the Cold War
B) the distribution of world power as it stood in 1945
C) the share of each region in the world's population
D) the votes cast by all members in the General Assembly
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) the distribution of world power as it stood in 1945
Why: The passage opens by saying the Council reflects the distribution of power as it stood in 1945.
Why not the others:
(A) The Cold War ended long after 1945.
(C) The passage says regions with large populations are poorly represented.
(D) The passage does not say the Council reflects Assembly votes.
Key point: The Council was designed for the world of 1945.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: Who the passage says is under-represented
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Any change, however, requires an amendment to the UN Charter, which must be approved by two-thirds of the members, including all five permanent members. This is why, despite years of debate, the Council looks much as it did decades ago.

Question: Which part of the world does the passage say is poorly represented in the Security Council?
options: A) Western Europe and North America
B) The five permanent members together
C) The states that founded the UN in 1945
D) Asia, Africa and Latin America
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Asia, Africa and Latin America
Why: The passage says many new members came from Asia, Africa and Latin America and that critics see the developing world as poorly represented.
Why not the others:
(A) These regions already hold several permanent seats.
(B) The permanent members dominate the Council.
(C) The founders' world of 1945 is what the Council reflects.
Key point: Reform is about fairer representation of the developing world.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: What the passage says about changing the veto
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

The structure of the UN Security Council still reflects the distribution of power in the world as it stood in 1945. Since then the membership of the United Nations has grown from 51 to 193 states, many of them newly independent countries of Asia, Africa and Latin America, yet the Council has been enlarged only once. Any change, however, requires an amendment to the UN Charter, which must be approved by two-thirds of the members, including all five permanent members. This is why, despite years of debate, the Council looks much as it did decades ago.

Question: What does the passage say about the veto?
options: A) It was abolished when the Council was enlarged.
B) All members agree it should be given to new members.
C) Some want it ended or limited, but the permanent five resist.
D) It can be used by any member of the Security Council.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Some want it ended or limited, but the permanent five resist.
Why: The passage says some want the veto abolished or limited, while the permanent members are unwilling to give it up.
Why not the others:
(A) The veto still exists.
(B) The passage describes disagreement, not agreement.
(D) Only the five permanent members have the veto.
Key point: The veto is the hardest part of reform.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: Statement that runs against the passage
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

The structure of the UN Security Council still reflects the distribution of power in the world as it stood in 1945. Since then the membership of the United Nations has grown from 51 to 193 states, many of them newly independent countries of Asia, Africa and Latin America, yet the Council has been enlarged only once. Critics say that the developing world is poorly represented in the body that takes the most important decisions on peace and security. The veto is an even harder question: some want it abolished or limited, while the permanent members are unwilling to give it up. India argues that, as the world's largest democracy, home to about one-fifth of humanity, with a growing economy and a long record in peacekeeping, it should be a permanent member. Any change, however, requires an amendment to the UN Charter, which must be approved by two-thirds of the members, including all five permanent members. This is why, despite years of debate, the Council looks much as it did decades ago.

Question: Which of the following runs against what the passage says?
options: A) The Council has grown in step with the growth of the UN's membership.
B) The UN's membership has risen from 51 to 193 states since 1945.
C) India bases its claim partly on its record in UN peacekeeping.
D) Members disagree about the criteria for choosing new members.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The Council has grown in step with the growth of the UN's membership.
Why: The passage says the Council has been enlarged only once even though membership grew from 51 to 193, so (A) contradicts it.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) are each stated in the passage.
Key point: The Council has not kept pace with the General Assembly.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: Why reform of the Council is so slow
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

The structure of the UN Security Council still reflects the distribution of power in the world as it stood in 1945. Since then the membership of the United Nations has grown from 51 to 193 states, many of them newly independent countries of Asia, Africa and Latin America, yet the Council has been enlarged only once. Critics say that the developing world is poorly represented in the body that takes the most important decisions on peace and security. Proposals for reform include adding new permanent members, adding more non-permanent members, or both, and there is a long debate about which criteria should decide who deserves a seat. The veto is an even harder question: some want it abolished or limited, while the permanent members are unwilling to give it up. India argues that, as the world's largest democracy, home to about one-fifth of humanity, with a growing economy and a long record in peacekeeping, it should be a permanent member. Any change, however, requires an amendment to the UN Charter, which must be approved by two-thirds of the members, including all five permanent members. This is why, despite years of debate, the Council looks much as it did decades ago.

Question: What best explains, according to the passage, why the Council has changed so little?
options: A) The General Assembly has never discussed the question of reform.
B) The developing countries do not want any more seats on the Council.
C) India has withdrawn its claim to a permanent seat on the Council.
D) Charter changes need all five permanent members to agree to them.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Charter changes need all five permanent members to agree to them.
Why: The passage says any change needs a Charter amendment approved by two-thirds of members, including all five permanent members, who can block it.
Why not the others:
(A) The passage speaks of years of debate.
(B) Critics from the developing world want more representation.
(C) The passage says India continues to press its claim.
Key point: The permanent five hold the key to their own reform.
